title: Availability and what I am looking for
text:
I am a second-year B.Tech student, so I graduate in 2028. Right now I am on a paid internship at
Open Computer, so I am not immediately available full-time, but I am the kind of candidate who
can start on a part-time or internship basis and is looking for a team to grow with.

What I want from a role is to be somewhere that is genuinely working on the cutting edge of
human technology, and where I would own real surface area early rather than a narrow ticket.

The honest way to put it: I would rather be somewhere that treats AI as a real engineering
surface with users and failure modes, not as a feature checkbox.

title: Google professional certifications
text:
I completed two Google professional certificates through Coursera, both in June 2026.

The Google Project Management Professional Certificate covered project lifecycle management, risk
mitigation, budgeting, and scope and stakeholder management.

The Google AI Essentials certificate covered prompt engineering, generative AI for business, data

They are professional certificates rather than degrees, and I would rather overstate what they

title: How to reach Sankalp
text:
I read everything that reaches me, eventually.

The site has a `/contact` command with my email, LinkedIn and GitHub. Use that — the addresses

I am based in Bengaluru, India, which matters mostly for timezone if you want to set up a call.

title: B.Tech in Digital Transformation at Atria University
text:
I am studying a B.Tech in Digital Transformation (Computer Science) at Atria University in
Bengaluru. I started in August 2024 and graduate in August 2028, so I am in my second year.

The degree deliberately mixes computer science with product and business. My coursework covers
data structures and algorithms, relational databases and SQL, full-stack web development on
both frontend and backend, supervised and unsupervised machine learning, and deep learning. On
the product side it covers design thinking, agile sprint methodology, AI-driven problem solving,
and financial modeling.

That combination is why my projects tend to be end-to-end. The product coursework is the part
that pushes me to finish and ship something rather than leaving it working in a notebook.

title: schooling before Atria University
text:
Before Atria University I went through Greenwood High International School in Bengaluru, where
I did the International Baccalaureate Diploma Programme from August 2022 to May 2024, following
IGCSE from April 2021 to May 2022.

Before that I was at Hillgrove Secondary School and Shuqun Primary School, both in Singapore.

title: What Sankalp owns at Open Computer, specifically
text:
At Open Computer I do three things that are unusual together for one person.

First, frontend and design development for an LLM-based agent product. I ship the product UI
end to end, not just components of it.

Second, I built the design system around an ASCII-based image design language. The reason for
going ASCII rather than pixels is cross-context compatibility and performance: the same visual
vocabulary survives being rendered in a terminal, in a chat bubble, in a log, and on a slow
connection, without redrawing anything.

Third, I designed the workflow that governs how the agent exercises curiosity and
discoverability. That is the part of agent design that is not about the model at all — it is
about what the agent is allowed to go look at, and when.

title: Internship as Member of Technical Staff at Open Computer
text:
Since May 2026 I have worked as a Member of Technical Staff (intern) at Open Computer, in
Bengaluru. It is a four-person team.

I own frontend and design development for the company's LLM-based agent product. Concretely
that means I build the design system the product is rendered with, and I designed and set up the
workflow that defines how the agent exercises curiosity and discoverability — that is, how it
decides what to go and look at next rather than only answering what it was asked.

The work is on deliverables slated for the public beta launch, so most of the specifics are
under trade-secret protection and I cannot go into them. I can talk about the shape of the work
and the problems it poses.

title: Who Sankalp Krishnamurthy is and what he is doing now
text:
I am Sankalp Krishnamurthy, a B.Tech student in Digital Transformation (Computer Science) at
Atria University in Bengaluru, India, graduating in 2028. I am in my second year.

Right now I split my time between a paid internship and my own projects. At Open Computer I am
a Member of Technical Staff on a four-person team. Outside of that I build end-to-end AI
products myself, mostly things that combine a model with a real interface someone can actually
use.

I like working at the edge of what software is supposed to look like. The pattern I enjoy most
is taking a capability that normally lives in a notebook or a CLI and turning it into something
a non-specialist can drive.

Beyond that: philosophy, where I am opinionated enough that people tell me not to argue about it,

That is not why I built this site, but it is not a coincidence either.

title: MIDI.ai — the parts Sankalp wrote himself
text:
The models in the pipeline are off the shelf. The code that makes them a pipeline is mine.

I wrote the orchestrator that sequences the five stages and passes data between them, the
YAMNet-to-General-MIDI program mapper — a 40-entry lookup translating what the timbre classifier
calls a sound into the GM program number a DAW expects — the post-processor that cleans up the
transcription into something playable, and the CLI wrapper.

So the model selection is borrowed and well-informed, but the thing that makes the stages
compose into a usable result is original.

title: MIDI.ai — the five-stage pipeline
text:
MIDI.ai runs as a divide-and-conquer pipeline of five stages.

One, stem isolation with a Hybrid Transformer Demucs v4 in PyTorch, which splits the mix into
separate sources. Two, Librosa MIR analysis for tempo, key and tuning. Three, YAMNet for timbre
classification. Four, Spotify Basic Pitch for the actual note transcription. Five, PrettyMIDI
for post-processing into a clean, playable file.

Every stage is chosen to do the one thing it is good at. Nothing is asked to be good at two
things, which is why the stages are separate processes rather than one fused model.

title: MIDI.ai — what it is and why it exists
text:
MIDI.ai is a pipeline that turns polyphonic audio into a MIDI file. I started it in December 2025
and have been building it solo.

The problem it solves is that converting a finished music track into editable MIDI is genuinely
hard when more than one instrument is playing. A single-note transcription model will happily
output something, but the result is a flat smear that is not usable in a DAW. MIDI.ai is built
around the assumption that you have to separate the track before you can transcribe it, and that
the separation step is where most of the quality is won or lost.

It is written in Python and is modular, so each stage can be run, inspected, and replaced on its
own.

title: Open Slides — features I owned, and the honest limitation
text:
On Open Slides I owned the Template Gallery end to end: the schema behind it, the server-rendered
browse page, and the `UsePromptModal` including its fork path. I also did the home-page work —
a rose-particle hero, accessibility, and responsive layout.

Export goes to PDF as vector and to PPTX rasterised, both through the `pdf-server` on the VPS.

The honest limitation: the StackBlitz WebContainer integration only works in desktop Chromium.
It does not run on mobile browsers. That was a deliberate trade — a real in-browser runtime was
worth more than mobile reach for the people who actually use it.

Testing discipline is Vitest plus `tsc --noEmit` on every change.

title: Open Slides — the technical stack and the parts I built myself
text:
Open Slides runs on Next.js 16 with the App Router, React 19, TypeScript and Tailwind. Styling
is driven by a custom CSS-variable design-token system rather than utility values scattered
through components.

The part I am most opinionated about is the model routing. Instead of calling a model provider
SDK directly, I wrote an in-house proxy called `claude-router` that sits in front of the
provider and routes across Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.7 and Haiku 4.5. Every model call in the product
goes through it, which means the routing decision is mine and it can change without touching
product code.

The agent loop streams over SSE, and there is a prompt flow with a five-dimension self-critique
gate before output is accepted.

title: Open Slides — what it is
text:
Open Slides is an end-to-end AI presentation platform, and it is the largest thing I have built
on my own. I started it in March 2026 and I am still working on it.

The idea is that you talk to it. A chat-driven agent builds, edits, and exports slide decks,
documents, sheets, and websites in real time. Not a generator that hands you a file at the end —
an agent loop you stay in conversation with while the artefact changes underneath you.

It is deployed on Vercel. I have also written a `pdf-server` that runs on a VPS, which is what
handles the heavier export work.

title: Open Computer — the product Sankalp works on
text:
Open Computer is the company I intern at, and the product is a platform for discovering AI
skills and plugins. The idea is that there is a rapidly growing supply of agent capabilities and
no good way to find the one you want, so the product is about curiosity and discoverability.

I have been on this since May 2026, working on the frontend and design. I have written about my
specific responsibilities separately, because the interesting part is not the product description
but what I actually own.

title: The Procrastination Engine
text:
The Procrastination Engine is a clock made of several tiny clocks. It is time within a time
within a time — each layer tracks and renders the one inside it.

I built it in October 2025 for fun, in JavaScript with Canvas. It is the one project here with no
strategic justification whatsoever, and I like it for that.

title: Backend and runtime skills
text:
On the backend I use Node.js with Express, and I have been getting into Bun.

The work I do here is usually not heavy API plumbing. It is the layer that sits between a model
and a user: proxying and routing model calls, streaming responses, and holding the state of an
agent loop while it runs. On Open Slides that is the `claude-router` proxy I wrote, which routes
across three Claude models and streams over SSE.

For hosting I have shipped to Vercel and to a VPS, and I run a `pdf-server` on a VPS for the
heavier document export work in Open Slides.

title: Cloud and database skills
text:
I have working experience across all three major clouds — AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud
Platform — at roughly the same level, which honestly means I have breadth and not much depth in
any one of them.

On the data side I use PostgreSQL, MongoDB and SQL. The SQL is coursework and project work rather
than deep database engineering; I know how to model a schema and write the queries, and I know
what an index is for.

One piece of infrastructure I have actually leaned on hard is Cloudflare. This site is a static
Astro build on Cloudflare Pages, and the `/ask` command behind this answer runs on a Cloudflare
Worker with Vectorize and Workers AI.

title: Frontend skills
text:
On the frontend I work primarily in React, and more recently React 19 with Next.js 16 using the
App Router. I use TypeScript throughout and Tailwind for styling, with custom CSS-variable design
tokens underneath so the token layer stays separate from the utility layer.

This site — the one you are reading this answer on — is a good example of what I do when I own
the whole thing end to end. It is an Astro site with a WebGPU particle system and a 2D Canvas
fallback, built as a terminal interface.

Design is not a separate skill from frontend for me. On Open Slides and at Open Computer I own
both, including the design systems.

title: LLM agent design experience
text:
I design LLM agents, and I have shipped two quite different kinds.

Open Slides is a chat-driven agent loop that builds and edits artefacts in real time — slides,
documents, sheets, websites — with a self-critique gate before output is accepted.

Open Computer is the opposite problem: not generating, but deciding what to go and look at. I
designed the workflow that governs how that agent exercises curiosity and discoverability, which
is an agent-design problem with no generation step in it at all.

I also wrote `claude-router`, an in-house proxy that routes across Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.7 and
Haiku 4.5, so I have direct experience of multi-model routing as a design problem rather than a
config file.

title: Machine learning and audio ML experience
text:
I work hands-on with PyTorch, TensorFlow and Librosa, and I have used them on real problems
rather than only tutorials.

The concrete instance is MIDI.ai, where I use a Hybrid Transformer Demucs v4 for stem separation,
Spotify Basic Pitch for note transcription, and YAMNet for timbre classification. Choosing those
three means knowing what each model is actually good at and putting the right one on the right
stage, which I think is more the skill than any single model's architecture.

I would describe myself as strong on applied audio and pipeline work and still developing on
training models from scratch. I have used pre-trained models intelligently; I have not published
a novel architecture.

title: Programming languages Sankalp works in
text:
I work in JavaScript, TypeScript, Python and Java as my main languages, and I rate all four as
solid working proficiency rather than expert.

Rust I am learning. It is not something I would want to be handed a production service in yet.

I also do a lot of work in data structures and algorithms. That is coursework at Atria
University, but it is also the thing that makes the pipeline work I do possible — a lot of
audio and agent work is really graph and scheduling problems wearing a costume.

title: How Sankalp works
text:
Team collaboration and leadership are my strongest non-technical skills. I rate problem solving
as solid and project management as something I am actively improving — which is a fair summary
of someone who ships well inside a small team but is still building the habit of running larger
planning cycles.

Working in a four-person team at Open Computer has been the main thing that taught me this. It is
small enough that you own a whole surface area, which means you cannot hide behind a narrow
specialisation, and you have to talk to the people who depend on what you build.

I work in agile sprints. Design thinking and AI-driven problem solving are both part of my
formal training, and the Digital Transformation degree leans on that combination deliberately.
